quickReference.title: Argumentative & Source-Based Essays and Revision
quickReference.purpose: Anchors essay thesis design, logical paragraph architecture, counterargument handling, and high-yield revision rules.
checklist: Verify whether the essay task requires an independent argumentative essay or a source-based informative/explanatory synthesis of two provided texts.
Confirm that every body paragraph opens with a focused topic sentence tied directly to the thesis and develops one clear point with specific support.
On revision items, check purpose, audience, logical flow, and conciseness before tweaking surface wording.
formulas: Argumentative essay blueprint: Thesis (clear debatable claim plus reasoning) → 2 to 3 developed body paragraphs (claim, concrete example/evidence, analysis) → Counterargument plus respectful rebuttal → Concise conclusion.

Source-based essay blueprint: Objective synthesis thesis → Balanced integration of both sources (paraphrase and brief attributed quotes) → Thematic organization comparing/connecting both texts → Zero personal opinion unless prompted.
Paragraph cohesion formula: Topic Sentence + Logical Transition + Specific Evidence + Analytical Commentary linking back to the central thesis.
Concision and clarity hierarchy: prefer active voice, strong verbs, and direct phrasing over wordy nominalizations, redundant pairs (each and every, past history), and off-topic tangents.
decisionRules: When a revision question asks whether to keep or delete a sentence → delete sentences that repeat earlier facts or drift away from the paragraph's controlling idea, even if they are factually interesting.

When choosing the best transition between two paragraphs → read the final idea of paragraph one and the core claim of paragraph two, then match the exact logical relation (contrast, cause, addition, or example).
When drafting the Praxis Core source-based essay → synthesize both sources around shared themes rather than summarizing Source 1 in full followed by Source 2 with no connection.
When a sentence-combining item offers four grammatical versions → choose the concise option that subordinates the less important idea and preserves the intended logical emphasis.
cautions: Do not turn a source-based explanatory essay into a personal opinion rant or ignore one of the two required source passages.
Never lift full sentences verbatim from source passages without quotation marks and clear attribution, as unattributed copying lowers essay scores.
Avoid selecting a transition that sounds formal (consequently, nevertheless) if it contradicts the actual relationship between the two sentences.

quickReference.title: Standard English Conventions, Usage & Research Literacy
quickReference.purpose: Anchors grammar, punctuation, sentence boundary, and academic research/citation rules for Praxis Core Writing.
checklist: Strip away prepositional phrases and nonessential clauses to pair the true grammatical subject with its verb and pronoun.
Inspect every comma, semicolon, and colon to confirm whether the clauses on each side are independent or dependent.
For research items, check whether the source is primary vs. secondary, peer-reviewed vs. commercial, current, and directly relevant to the research question.
formulas: Clause boundary rules: Independent + comma + FANBOYS + Independent; Independent + semicolon + Independent; Independent + colon + list/explanation (never place a colon directly after a verb or preposition).

Agreement and modifier rules: indefinite pronouns each, everyone, neither, and everybody take singular verbs/pronouns; introductory participial modifiers must immediately precede the subject performing the action.

Parallelism and verb consistency: items in a series or paired with correlative conjunctions (not only/but also, either/or, neither/nor) must share grammatical form; maintain verb tense unless time shifts.

Research credibility & citation benchmarks: primary sources offer firsthand data or original artifacts; secondary sources interpret them; paraphrased ideas and data still require citation, whereas widely known common knowledge does not.
decisionRules: When two independent clauses are joined only by a comma (comma splice) or by however with commas → replace the comma before the second clause with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus coordinating conjunction.

When a sentence begins with a modifying phrase (such as Walking into the lab, the microscope looked dusty) → verify that the noun immediately after the comma performs the action; otherwise fix the dangling modifier.

When selecting the best research source for an academic claim → prioritize peer-reviewed journals, university/government data, and primary records over anonymous blogs, wikis, or commercially biased sites.

When asked whether a paraphrase needs a citation → always require attribution whenever specific findings, arguments, statistics, or structures come from an outside source, even if every word is rephrased.
cautions: Do not be fooled by a plural noun inside a prepositional phrase (The collection of rare manuscripts IS, not ARE) or by phrases like along with and as well as.

Never choose No Error without checking commonly overlooked traps: singular-to-plural pronoun shifts (a student paired with they in strict formal stems), who vs. whom, its vs. it's, affect (verb) vs. effect (noun), and faulty comparisons.
Avoid using a semicolon to join a dependent clause to an independent clause.

quickReference.title: Number Operations, Ratios, Percents & Measurement
quickReference.purpose: Anchors arithmetic properties, proportional reasoning, percent change, exponent rules, and unit conversion formulas.
checklist: Confirm the exact target quantity and unit requested (percent increase vs. final price, total time vs. rate, exact fraction vs. rounded decimal).
Estimate the magnitude first using friendly benchmark numbers (10%, 25%, 50%, powers of 10) to catch decimal-place errors.
Verify that ratios and proportions keep matching units aligned across numerators and denominators before cross-multiplying.
formulas: Percent & change formulas: Part = Percent × Whole; Percent Change = ((New − Original) / Original) × 100%; successive changes multiply factors (for example, +20% then −20% equals 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96, a net 4% decrease).
Rates & interest: Distance = Rate × Time (Average Speed = Total Distance / Total Time); Simple Interest I = P × r × t and Total A = P(1 + rt); Annual Compound Interest A = P(1 + r)^t.
Exponent & scientific notation laws: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n); a^m / a^n = a^(m−n); (a^m)^n = a^(mn); a^0 = 1 (for a ≠ 0); a^(−n) = 1 / a^n; scientific notation a × 10^n with 1 ≤ a below 10.
Key measurement conversions: 1 ft = 12 in; 1 yd = 3 ft; 1 mi = 5,280 ft; 1 lb = 16 oz; 1 gal = 4 qt = 8 pt = 16 cups; 1 km = 1,000 m; 1 m = 100 cm = 1,000 mm; 1 kg = 1,000 g; 1 L = 1,000 mL.
decisionRules: When a problem gives a discounted price and asks for the original price → divide the sale price by (1 − discount rate) rather than adding the discount percentage back onto the sale price.

When converting squared or cubed units (such as square feet to square yards or cubic centimeters to cubic meters) → apply the linear conversion factor twice for area (k^2) and three times for volume (k^3).
When asked for average speed over a two-leg trip at different speeds → compute total distance divided by total time rather than averaging the two rates.
When an item states part-to-part ratio a:b and asks for one part of a total T → divide T by (a + b) to find one share, then multiply by the target part.
cautions: Never divide by the new value instead of the original value when computing percent increase or percent decrease.
Do not perform addition before subtraction or multiplication before division blindly; within PEMDAS, multiplication/division and addition/subtraction evaluate strictly left to right.
Watch negative base exponents carefully: (−3)^2 equals +9, whereas −3^2 equals −9.

quickReference.title: Descriptive Statistics, Sampling & Probability
quickReference.purpose: Anchors measures of center and spread, distribution shape, study design validity, and probability rules.
checklist: Verify whether a data table or frequency chart lists individual values or grouped counts/weights before computing mean or median.
Check whether events are mutually exclusive or overlapping, and whether draws occur with replacement (independent) or without replacement (dependent).
Inspect sample selection method (random vs. convenience/voluntary) and study design (observational vs. randomized experiment) before drawing conclusions.
formulas: Center & spread: Mean = (Sum of values) / n; Median = middle ordered value (average of two middle values when n is even); Range = Max − Min; Interquartile Range IQR = Q3 − Q1 (middle 50% of data).

Distribution shape & resistance: Mean and standard deviation are sensitive to outliers; Median and IQR are resistant; right-skewed distributions pull Mean above Median, while left-skewed pull Mean below Median.

Core probability rules: P(A) = Favorable / Total equally likely outcomes; Complement P(not A) = 1 − P(A); Addition P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); Fundamental Counting Principle multiplies choices m × n.

Compound events & inference: Independent P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B); Dependent P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B given A); random sampling enables generalization to a population, while random assignment supports causal inference.
decisionRules: When a dataset contains an extreme outlier or strong skew → choose Median and IQR rather than Mean and Range to describe typical performance and spread.
When a weighted average or missing-score problem gives the target mean → multiply target mean by total count n to find the required sum, then subtract the known scores.
When calculating P(at least one) across multiple trials → compute 1 − P(none) rather than summing overlapping cases.
When a study observes correlation in a non-random or self-selected survey → reject causal claims and reject broad population generalizations.
cautions: Never forget to order the dataset from least to greatest before identifying the median or quartiles Q1 and Q3.
Do not forget to subtract P(A and B) when two events can occur simultaneously (such as drawing a red card or a face card).
Avoid confusing a box plot median line with the mean, or assuming a wider box section contains more data points (each quartile holds 25% of observations).

quickReference.title: Linear/Quadratic Algebra, Functions & 2D/3D Geometry
quickReference.purpose: Anchors equations, slopes, functions, angle theorems, triangle relationships, and area/surface-area/volume formulas.
checklist: Check whether the prompt asks for x itself, an expression like 2x + 5, a radius vs. diameter, or surface area vs. volume.
Verify signs when distributing negatives, moving terms across an equals sign, or dividing an inequality by a negative number.
Sketch and label given dimensions, right angles, and parallel/congruent marks on geometry problems before choosing a formula.
formulas: Linear & coordinate algebra: Slope m = (y2 − y1) / (x2 − x1); Slope-intercept y = mx + b; Point-slope y − y1 = m(x − x1); Parallel slopes m1 = m2, Perpendicular m1 × m2 = −1; Distance d = sqrt((x2 − x1)^2 + (y2 − y1)^2); Midpoint ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2).

Quadratics & functions: For ax^2 + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0), Quadratic Formula x = (−b ± sqrt(b^2 − 4ac)) / (2a), vertex at x = −b / (2a); a relation is a function iff every input x maps to exactly one output y (vertical line test).

2D geometry & angles: Triangle area A = (1/2)bh, angle sum 180°, Pythagorean theorem a^2 + b^2 = c^2; Trapezoid A = (1/2)(b1 + b2)h; Circle C = 2πr = πd and A = πr^2; Convex n-gon interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°.

3D solids & scaling: Rectangular prism V = lwh, SA = 2(lw + lh + wh); Cylinder V = πr^2h, SA = 2πr^2 + 2πrh; Cone V = (1/3)πr^2h; Pyramid V = (1/3)Bh; Sphere V = (4/3)πr^3; Similar figures with scale k scale lengths by k, areas by k^2, volumes by k^3.
decisionRules: When solving an inequality and multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative value → flip the inequality direction immediately.
When a system of two linear equations has identical slopes and identical y-intercepts → identify infinitely many solutions; identical slopes with different intercepts indicate zero solutions.
When a circle problem provides the diameter d → divide by 2 to get radius r before computing A = πr^2 or cylinder/cone/sphere volume.
When two triangles share two congruent angles (AA similarity) → set up proportional corresponding sides to solve for the unknown length.
cautions: Never distribute an exponent over addition: (x + y)^2 equals x^2 + 2xy + y^2, not x^2 + y^2.
Do not confuse horizontal lines (slope = 0, equation y = c) with vertical lines (undefined slope, equation x = c).
Avoid mixing up area (square units) with perimeter/circumference (linear units) or forgetting the 1/3 factor on cones and pyramids.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Confusing Main Idea with a Narrow Detail or Extreme Inference
misconceptionFamilies.description: Selecting an answer choice that restates a single supporting example or introduces a sweeping, unsupported claim ("always," "proves," "solely") instead of synthesizing the central thesis that every paragraph of the Praxis Core reading passage actually supports.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Test each main-idea or inference choice against the whole passage: eliminate choices that cover only one sentence, contradict a concession, or leap past the author's stated evidence using extreme qualifiers.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Misreading Author Tone and Rhetorical Purpose
misconceptionFamilies.description: Choosing an emotionally exaggerated tone label ("outraged," "dismissive," "enthusiastic") when the passage uses measured academic qualification ("cautiously optimistic," "analytical"), or confusing what a paragraph says literally with why the author placed it in the argument.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Track hedging verbs, contrast transitions ("however," "although," "yet"), and structural pivots to separate literal topic content from rhetorical function and calibrated authorial attitude.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Missing Dangling Modifiers, Subject-Verb Agreement, and Comma Splice Traps
misconceptionFamilies.description: Approving sentences where an introductory participial phrase modifies the wrong noun, a verb agrees with a nearby prepositional-phrase noun instead of the true subject, or two independent clauses are joined with only a comma (often before "however" or "therefore").
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Strip intervening prepositional phrases to pair subject and verb directly, verify that the noun immediately following an opening modifier performs its action, and test both sides of every comma for complete independent clauses.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Applying Additive Scaling to Ratios and Using the Wrong Percent Base
misconceptionFamilies.description: Solving ratio or recipe problems by adding the same constant to both quantities instead of multiplying by a constant scale factor, or computing percent increase, percent decrease, or reverse-percent original price against the ending value instead of the original base.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Anchor every ratio problem to a multiplicative unit rate (k = y / x) and write every percent change over the starting quantity: percent change = (new − original) / original, and reverse-discount original = sale price / (1 − r).

misconceptionFamilies.label: Sign Distribution Errors, Inequality Flips, and Swapped Slope-Intercept Roles
misconceptionFamilies.description: Dropping a negative sign when distributing across parentheses, forgetting to reverse an inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number, inverting run-over-rise in slope calculations, or confusing the fixed y-intercept with the per-unit rate of change.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Distribute the signed coefficient explicitly to every term inside parentheses, check whether an inequality step divides by a negative value, compute slope as (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁) with matched point order, and label b as starting cost and m as rate per unit.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Mean vs. Median Distortion, Sampling Overreach, and Geometry Dimension Confusion
misconceptionFamilies.description: Treating the arithmetic mean as resistant to extreme outliers, overgeneralizing from convenience or non-random samples, reading truncated graph axes literally, or mixing up 1D perimeter/circumference, 2D area, 3D volume, and linear vs. area scale factors.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Check data skewness before choosing median over mean, verify random sampling vs. random assignment before claiming population or causal scope, inspect graph axis origins, and match every geometric formula and scale factor to its exact dimension (k, k², or k³).

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Confusing Main Idea with a Narrow Detail or Extreme Inference
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Filter Out Narrow Details and Extreme Inferences in Core Reading
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A reading stem asks for the primary purpose, central claim, or best-supported inference, and tempting distractors either copy a true one-sentence fact verbatim or slip in extreme words like "all," "never," "proves," or "only."
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does this choice cover the unifying claim across the entire passage while staying strictly inside the evidence the author actually gave?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Tag each reading option with one of four labels—True-but-Narrow Detail, Extreme Overreach, Outside Assumption, or Passage-Wide Synthesis—before comparing phrasing.
stages.requiredOutput: Quote the exact word or phrase (such as "proves," "eliminates," or a single-example noun) that exposes each distractor as too narrow or too extreme.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Draft a one-sentence passage umbrella statement ("The author argues/explains X while noting qualification Y") and contrast it with an unsupported inference leap.
stages.requiredOutput: Write a two-part validity test: every valid main idea must absorb both the central claim and any major concession, and every valid inference must be logically forced by stated lines.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Evaluate a short passage describing a town rail-to-trail project that increased foot traffic while raising maintenance costs, then sort four candidate summaries into Narrow Detail, Extreme Inference, Reversed Claim, and Best Central Idea.
stages.requiredOutput: Assign each of the four candidate statements to its category and cite the passage phrase that confirms the balanced central idea.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Apply the umbrella-and-evidence check to a fresh paired or informational passage where an attractive distractor repeats exact vocabulary from paragraph two.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the choice supported across the full text and state why the vocabulary-matching detail option fails the passage-wide scope test.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Misreading Author Tone and Rhetorical Purpose
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Calibrate Author Tone and Distinguish Content from Rhetorical Function
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A craft-and-structure item asks why the author mentions a study, counterexample, or metaphor—or asks for the author's attitude—and one distractor names an extreme emotion while another merely summarizes the quoted sentence without explaining its job.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: What rhetorical job does this sentence perform for the surrounding argument (concede, qualify, illustrate, contrast), and how strong or restrained is the author's wording?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Highlight every attitude marker (qualifiers such as "perhaps," "bridge technology," "quietly daring") and every structural hinge ("although," "for example," "however") around the referenced lines.
stages.requiredOutput: List the exact lexical cues showing whether the author's tone is neutral, cautiously evaluative, skeptical, or appreciative rather than hostile or ecstatic.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Convert a "what it says" paraphrase into a "why it is there" rhetorical-verb statement using precise function verbs (illustrate, qualify, anticipate an objection, contrast two approaches).
stages.requiredOutput: Write a paired contrast showing why "reports winter sampling" is literal content whereas "qualifies the generalizability of the study's recommendation" is rhetorical purpose.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Analyze two Core-style excerpts—one calling a budget proposal "ambitious, perhaps too ambitious" and another describing a street closure feared by merchants that later boosted sales—and match each to its calibrated tone and function.
stages.requiredOutput: Provide the precise tone pair (measured skepticism vs. evidence-backed rebuttal) and reject one overly emotional distractor for each excerpt.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-test on a two-paragraph passage where paragraph one diagnoses a problem and paragraph two weighs trade-offs of a remedy, plus a writing-tone revision item with sarcastic wording.
stages.requiredOutput: Identify the structural relationship between paragraphs and revise the sarcastic phrasing into objective academic prose suitable for educated adult readers.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Missing Dangling Modifiers, Subject-Verb Agreement, and Comma Splice Traps
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Run the Clause-Boundary, Subject-Core, and Modifier-Anchor Audit
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A Writing multiple-choice item looks smooth to the ear because a plural noun sits right before a plural verb, an opening "-ing" phrase sits next to an inanimate object, or ", however," glues two complete sentences together.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Who is the true grammatical subject after deleting prepositional phrases, who performs the opening modifier's action, and can both sides of the comma stand alone as complete sentences?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Inspect every Writing stem with three quick markers: cross out prepositional phrases ("of the committees"), box the noun immediately after any introductory comma, and run a period test at every internal comma.
stages.requiredOutput: Name which of the three grammar traps (agreement distractor noun, dangling/misplaced modifier, or comma splice/run-on) is embedded in the sentence.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Review the four legal clause joins (period, semicolon, comma + FANBOYS coordinating conjunction, or subordination) and verify why conjunctive adverbs ("however," "therefore," "moreover") require a semicolon or period before them.
stages.requiredOutput: Write the corrected rule set: semicolon + conjunctive adverb + comma for independent clauses, and noun-actor immediately following an introductory participial phrase.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Repair three flawed sentences: (1) "The box of archival photographs were damaged." (2) "Walking through the gallery, the new exhibit impressed the visitors." (3) "The pilot shortened wait times, however, staffing costs rose."
stages.requiredOutput: Produce the grammatically repaired version of each sentence and state the exact rule applied to each fix.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Audit a multi-error Core Writing item combining parallel structure, pronoun-antecedent clarity, and semicolon usage so that no single surface check misses a secondary error.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the completely error-free sentence and explain the specific flaw that disqualifies each of the remaining options.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Applying Additive Scaling to Ratios and Using the Wrong Percent Base
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Lock In Multiplicative Scaling and Original-Base Percent Equations
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A ratio, map-scale, unit-rate, or discount/markup item tempts you to add the difference between two numbers ("3 cups for 2 batches → add 3 to get 6 cups for 5 batches") or to compute a 25% markup and 25% discount as canceling each other out.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: What is the constant multiplicative rate per 1 unit, and which quantity is the 100% original base before the percent change occurred?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Spot additive-thinking traps in proportions and base-switching traps in percent problems (discount-to-original, successive percents, and percent increase vs. decrease).
stages.requiredOutput: Identify the exact unit ratio (such as cups per batch or miles per inch) and label which number represents 100% (the original base) before computing.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Contrast additive change (adding +3 to both numerator and denominator breaks equivalence) with multiplicative scaling (multiplying both by 5/2), and write the multiplier model for percent change: final = original × (1 ± r).
stages.requiredOutput: Show with a numeric check why a 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease yields 0.96 of the original (not 1.00) because the second base is larger.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Solve three Core Number & Quantity problems step by step: (1) 3 cups of flour for 2 batches scaled to 5 batches, (2) a $60 sale price after a 25% discount to find the original price, and (3) a 1 inch : 12 miles map scaled to 3.5 inches.
stages.requiredOutput: Show the unit-rate or multiplier equation for each item (7.5 cups, $80 original price, 42 miles) and verify each answer by plugging it back into the original context.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Solve a fresh percent-change and unit-conversion word problem (such as meters to centimeters combined with a rate comparison) without falling into an additive or reversed-base distractor.
stages.requiredOutput: State the scale multiplier, the 100% base, and the verified final quantity with matching units.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Sign Distribution Errors, Inequality Flips, and Swapped Slope-Intercept Roles
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Protect Signs, Inequality Direction, and Slope-Intercept Meaning
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: An algebra item contains parentheses preceded by a minus sign, an inequality with a negative coefficient on x, two coordinate points for slope, or a word problem combining a one-time fee with a recurring monthly charge.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Did every distributed term keep its signed product, did any division by a negative flip the inequality, and does the slope match vertical change divided by horizontal change?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Circle every negative sign before parentheses or variables, highlight whether the prompt asks for an expression vs. a solution set, and tag the fixed starting amount vs. the per-unit rate in linear word problems.
stages.requiredOutput: Flag the exact high-risk step (distribution sign, inequality flip, point-order subtraction, or m vs. b assignment) before solving.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Verify the four algebra guardrails: distribute a(bx − c) = abx − ac; reverse the inequality symbol whenever multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative; compute m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁) in consistent order; map y = mx + b so m carries the "per" unit and b is the value at x = 0.
stages.requiredOutput: Write one worked check showing why −2x + 6 ≥ 14 becomes x ≤ −4 (substituting x = −5 confirms 16 ≥ 14, whereas x = 0 fails).

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Work three Core Algebra items: expand 4(2x − 3) + 5, compute the slope through (0, 5) and (4, 13) and build the equation, and model a $12 signup fee plus $4 per month for m months.
stages.requiredOutput: Report 8x − 7, slope m = 2 with y = 2x + 5, and C = 4m + 12, including a quick substitution check for each result.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Solve a transfer item evaluating a quadratic function f(x) = 2x² − 3 at a negative input or solving a linear inequality with a negative coefficient, checking order of operations (exponent before multiplication).
stages.requiredOutput: Provide the solved value or solution set and confirm it with a test-point substitution.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Mean vs. Median Distortion, Sampling Overreach, and Geometry Dimension Confusion
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Separate Center, Sampling Scope, and 1D/2D/3D Geometry Measures
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A statistics item includes an extreme outlier, a truncated vertical axis starting at 95, or a volunteer sample claiming cause-and-effect—or a geometry item gives a radius or scale factor and slips perimeter/diameter/linear-scale distractors into an area or volume question.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Is the distribution skewed (favoring median over mean), does the study design support population generalization or causation, and does the geometric formula match 1D length, 2D area, or 3D volume?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Scan data prompts for outliers, axis-origin breaks, sample selection method, and margin-of-error wording; scan geometry prompts for radius vs. diameter and the target unit dimension (cm, cm², or cm³).
stages.requiredOutput: List the exact statistical distortion or dimensional mismatch that creates the primary distractor.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Pair each concept with its rule: outliers pull the mean toward the tail while leaving the median stable; random sampling supports generalizing to a population whereas random assignment supports causal inference; scaling every linear side by k multiplies perimeter by k, area by k², and volume by k³.
stages.requiredOutput: Build a compact reference table contrasting C = 2πr vs. A = πr², perimeter vs. area vs. prism volume (l × w × h), and mean vs. median sensitivity.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Solve three Core Data/Geometry items: (1) find the missing fourth score when the mean of four scores is 18 and three are 14, 17, and 21; (2) explain how a y-axis starting at 95 exaggerates bars of 98 and 100; (3) compute both the new side length and new area when a square of side 4 is enlarged by scale factor 3.
stages.requiredOutput: Report fourth score = 20 (total 72 − 52), note that a non-zero baseline inflates visual difference (5/3 ≈ 1.67× bar height for a ~2% numeric gap), and distinguish new side = 12 (×3) from new area = 144 (×9).

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Tackle a fresh probability, sampling, or right-triangle/circle item (such as radius 5 circumference vs. area, or margin of error 60% ± 4 percentage points) and verify units and interpretation bounds.
stages.requiredOutput: State the verified numeric or interpretive answer (such as 56% to 64% plausible interval, or 10π circumference vs. 25π area) and rule out the dimension-swapped distractor.
